units.title: Memory through the OS’s eyes
units.blurb: What the operating system sees when .NET asks for memory: virtual addresses and pages, reserve and commit, why a process has several "memory used" numbers, the stack limit and CPU caches.

lessons.title: Virtual memory
lessons.sub: Addresses, pages, the MMU and page faults

cards.title: An address in your program is not an address in RAM
cards.body:
When C# code reads an object’s field, the CPU gets an address like 0x7FF6_1234_5678. That’s a virtual address: it says nothing about which memory chip actually holds the bytes.

Every process has its own address space, a huge map of addresses that is almost entirely empty. On every access the CPU translates the virtual address into a physical one. The translation is done by a unit inside the CPU, the MMU, and the OS keeps the translation rules in the process’s page table.
cards.deep: Why bother: processes are isolated from each other, you can hand out more addresses than there is RAM, rarely used data can be moved out to disk, and a file can be mapped into memory as if it were an array. The OS’s own code lives in the same map, but in the half that user code cannot touch.

cards.title: Pages
cards.body:
Translating every byte separately would be far too expensive, so memory is split into pages, usually 4 KB (4096 bytes) each. Translation works in whole pages.

An address splits into two parts: the high bits are the page number, the low 12 bits are the offset inside the page (212 = 4096). For 0x7FF6_1234_5678 the offset is 0x678 and the page number is everything else.

A page table entry holds the physical page number plus flags: is the page in memory, is it writable, can code run from it, can user code access it.
cards.deep: On x86-64 the page table is a four-level tree, 9 address bits per level, plus 12 bits of offset: 48 bits in total. Walking the tree on every read would be slow, so finished translations are cached in the TLB, a small buffer inside the CPU. A TLB miss costs a table walk. There are also large pages: 2 MB and 1 GB on x86-64. The normal page size depends on the platform: 4 KB on x86-64, 16 KB on Macs with Apple Silicon, and on ARM64 Linux the kernel is built with 4, 16 or 64 KB pages. From .NET you can read it with Environment.SystemPageSize.

cards.q: How many low bits of an address hold the offset inside a 4 KB page?
cards.explain: 4096 is 2 to the power of 12, so an offset from 0 to 4095 fits in exactly 12 bits. The remaining bits are the page number.

cards.title: Page faults
cards.body:
What if the page table entry says "this page is not in memory"? The CPU stops the instruction and calls an OS handler: that’s a page fault. The OS works out what happened:

  • Soft (minor) fault: the data is already in RAM, or all it takes is a zeroed page. The OS fills in the table entry and that’s it. Cost: on the order of a microsecond.
  • Hard (major) fault: the page must be read from disk, from the page file or from a mapped file such as DLL code. Cost: from tens of microseconds on an SSD to milliseconds on an HDD.
  • The address maps to nothing: the OS reports an access error, an access violation on Windows, a SIGSEGV signal on Linux.

After a soft or hard fault the instruction runs again and the program notices nothing, except the time it lost.
cards.deep: The first touch of freshly allocated memory is a page fault too: that is the moment the OS hands out a zeroed page. On Linux you can see the counts with ps -o min_flt,maj_flt -p PID or in the output of /usr/bin/time -v; on Windows, in the process performance counters. A null dereference in .NET also starts as an access error: pages near address zero are never mapped, and the runtime turns that fault into a NullReferenceException.

cards.q: Match the event with what it means
pairs: The page is already in RAM, it only needs mapping
The page has to be read from disk
A cache of finished address translations

cards.title: One address, two processes
cards.body:
Run a program twice and print the address of the same variable: the numbers may match. There’s no conflict: each process has its own page table, and the same virtual page leads to different physical pages in each.

A process can’t even name another process’s memory: every address it uses is translated through its own table. That’s what isolation means.

The reverse happens too: one physical page can be visible in several processes. That’s how the OS shares the code of system libraries and the runtime: it’s loaded into RAM once and mapped into every process that needs it.
cards.deep: ASLR, the random placement of modules, stacks and heaps at startup, makes matching addresses rarer and gets in the way of attacks, but the rule stays the same. You can read another process’s memory only through the OS (ReadProcessMemory on Windows, process_vm_readv on Linux, with the right permissions) or by agreeing on shared memory up front; in .NET that’s MemoryMappedFile. Shared library pages are marked copy-on-write: a process that tries to write gets its own copy.

cards.q: Two processes write different numbers to the same virtual address at the same time. What does each of them read back?
options: Each reads its own number
Both read the number of whoever wrote last
The second process gets an access error

wrong.1: That would happen if the address were physical. But the processes have different page tables.
wrong.2: There’s no error: in each process the address maps to that process’s own page.

cards.explain: The same virtual address in two processes goes through two different page tables and ends up in different physical pages.

cards.title: How much is 64 bits
cards.body:
A pointer in a 64-bit process takes 8 bytes, but today’s x86-64 CPUs use only 48 bits of a virtual address, which is 256 TB. Half goes to the kernel and half to the process: 128 TB of user space on both Windows and Linux.

For comparison, a 32-bit process sees only 4 GB of addresses, and on Windows it gets 2 GB of them by default.

The takeaway: a 64-bit process practically never runs out of addresses. What runs out is something else: physical memory and how much the OS is willing to promise. That’s the next lesson.
cards.deep: The top 16 bits of a 48-bit address must repeat bit 47 (a canonical address), which is why user addresses look like 0x0000_7FFx_xxxx_xxxx and kernel addresses start with 0xFFFF. Newer CPUs support five-level page tables and 57-bit addresses; Linux then hands out addresses above 128 TB only to programs that explicitly ask for them. A 32-bit process with the LargeAddressAware flag gets up to 4 GB on 64-bit Windows.

cards.q: A program reads a freshly allocated page for the first time. Put the steps in order
items: An instruction accesses a virtual address
The MMU finds no translation in the TLB and walks the page table
The entry is marked "not in memory", so the CPU raises a page fault
The OS takes a free physical page, zeroes it and fills in the entry
The instruction runs again and reads 0
cards.explain: This is a soft fault: no disk involved, the OS just finds a physical page and zeroes it. It zeroes it so the process can’t see someone else’s data.

cards.q: What is true about virtual memory? Select all that apply.
options: Every process has its own address space
The OS maps memory in whole pages
A virtual address is the same as a cell number in RAM
A hard page fault costs about as much as an L1 cache read
One physical page can be visible in several processes
cards.explain: A virtual address is translated through the page table and can lead anywhere. A hard fault is a disk read: it costs tens of thousands of times more than an L1 read, or worse.

cards.q: A RAM read takes on the order of 100 ns. How much longer does a hard page fault served from an SSD take?
options: About a thousand times longer or more
About twice as long
The same: both are memory
It’s faster: the disk caches
cards.explain: A hard fault from an SSD takes tens or hundreds of microseconds, three orders of magnitude more than a RAM access. With a spinning disk it’s milliseconds, another one or two orders worse. That’s why a program that runs short of RAM slows down so abruptly.

lessons.title: Reserve and commit
lessons.sub: Why a process has several different memory numbers

cards.title: Two steps: claim the addresses, then back them
cards.body:
Getting memory from the OS can take two steps.

Reserve: the process says "this range of addresses is mine". The OS just makes a note in the address space map. It costs neither RAM nor page file space.

Commit: the OS promises that the pages in the range will have something behind them, and counts them against a global limit made up of RAM plus the page file. But a physical page still appears only on first touch, through that same soft page fault.
cards.deep: On Windows both steps are done by VirtualAlloc: the MEM_RESERVE flag reserves, MEM_COMMIT commits. The reverse operations are VirtualFree with MEM_DECOMMIT (give back the promise, keep the addresses) and MEM_RELEASE (give back the addresses). Reservations come in multiples of 64 KB, commits in pages. Touching a page that is reserved but not committed is an access error.

cards.q: Claim 1 GB of addresses, but back only the first 64 KB with memory
cards.code:
void* p = VirtualAlloc(null, 1 << 30, ___, PAGE_NOACCESS);
VirtualAlloc(p, 64 * 1024, ___, PAGE_READWRITE);
cards.explain: First the whole range is reserved, then the first 64 KB are committed. The other addresses are taken but cost nothing until someone commits them.

cards.title: Linux: mmap and overcommit
cards.body:
On Linux the same two steps go through mmap: a range mapped with PROT_NONE is the counterpart of a reservation, and mprotect with read and write access is the counterpart of a commit.

The big difference is overcommit. By default Linux doesn’t keep strict count of its promises: it refuses only obviously impossible requests and grants the rest, betting that not all of that memory will be needed at once. Physical pages appear on first touch, just as on Windows.

If RAM and swap do run out, there’s no exception: the kernel starts the OOM killer, which kills a process with SIGKILL. The process simply vanishes, with no stack trace and no catch.
cards.deep: The mode is set in /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory: 0 is the heuristic (default), 1 allows everything, 2 is strict accounting against CommitLimit from /proc/meminfo. In a container the cgroup sets its own ceiling: go over the memory limit and the kernel kills the process inside the container, while the orchestrator sees exit code 137 (128 plus the SIGKILL number).

cards.q: Why can a program on Linux die from lack of memory not at the moment it allocates, but later?
options: Pages are handed out on first touch, there may not be enough of them then, and the OOM killer comes
mmap always reports errors with a delay
The garbage collector postpones the allocation until the next collection
cards.explain: With overcommit, an allocation is only a promise. Real memory is needed at the first write, and if there is none, the kernel picks a victim and kills it.

cards.title: How much memory does the process use? Depends what you count
cards.body:
• Virtual size (VSZ on Linux): every address in use, reserved, committed or mapped from files. For a .NET process that’s hundreds of gigabytes, and that’s fine.
  • Private bytes (commit): committed memory that belongs to this process alone, what the OS has promised it. Grows when you leak.
  • Working set (RSS on Linux): pages sitting in physical memory right now, including shared library pages.

What’s promised hasn’t been touched yet, and what’s been touched the OS can evict, so the numbers drift apart. In the Memory column, Task Manager shows the private working set by default, which is yet another number.
cards.deep: The working set can shrink without the program doing anything: under pressure the OS takes pages away and they go to standby. If the process touches them again, bringing them back is a soft fault. On Linux the most precise view is /proc/PID/smaps_rollup: it has Rss, Pss (shared pages divided between the processes) and anonymous memory. The private working set on Windows is the working set without shared pages.

cards.q: Match each number with what it counts
pairs: Every address in use, even with no memory behind it
Committed memory of this process alone
Pages that are in RAM right now

cards.title: How the CLR gets memory for the heap
cards.body:
At startup the garbage collector reserves a large contiguous range of addresses, hundreds of gigabytes in a 64-bit process. Addresses are free, and the heap knows it has room to grow.

From there the heap commits memory in chunks as it grows, and after a collection it can hand unneeded chunks back to the OS (decommit). So:

  • the virtual size is huge from the first second;
  • private bytes follow the size of the heap;
  • the working set is whatever the program has touched recently.
cards.deep: Since .NET 7 the heap is made of regions: by default 4 MB for ordinary objects and 32 MB for large ones. The initial reservation for regions is 256 GB by default, more on machines with a very large amount of RAM; the GCRegionRange setting changes it. GCHeapHardLimit caps the heap; in a container with a memory limit it defaults to 75% of that limit. From code you can see the numbers through GC.GetGCMemoryInfo(): HeapSizeBytes, TotalCommittedBytes, TotalAvailableMemoryBytes.

cards.q: A service on .NET 9 shows a virtual size of 260 GB and a working set of 300 MB. What does that mean?
options: All is well: addresses are reserved, and about 300 MB sit in RAM
A 260 GB leak
The process wrote 260 GB to the page file
cards.explain: A huge virtual size in .NET is the address reservation for the heap. It uses neither RAM nor the page file. You hunt leaks by private bytes and the size of the managed heap.

cards.q: Which line shows how much of the process’s memory is in RAM right now?
cards.explain: WorkingSet64 is the working set, the pages in physical memory. VirtualMemorySize64 is all addresses, PrivateMemorySize64 is committed private memory, and GC.GetTotalMemory is how many bytes the GC estimates managed objects take.

cards.title: OutOfMemoryException with RAM to spare
cards.body:
OutOfMemoryException doesn’t mean "RAM ran out". Typical causes:

  • The commit limit is exhausted. Windows has already promised all of RAM and the page file to processes. Actual RAM use may be low, since the promises are untouched, but the OS won’t make new ones.
  • The GC heap limit is reached. In a container or with GCHeapHardLimit, the runtime throws at its own boundary even if the machine has gigabytes free.
  • No contiguous range of addresses. A 32-bit problem: 2–4 GB of addresses get fragmented and a big array has nowhere to go.
  • The object is too big. An array longer than Array.MaxLength can’t be created no matter how much memory you have.

And on Linux without limits it may never get as far as an exception: the OOM killer kills the process.
cards.deep: Before an operation that is certain to need a lot of memory, you can ask in advance: MemoryFailPoint checks whether there’s room and throws InsufficientMemoryException before the work starts rather than halfway through. If OOM hits a 64-bit process on a big server, first check the container limits and the GC settings in runtimeconfig.json.

cards.q: What can cause an OutOfMemoryException while Task Manager shows gigabytes of free RAM? Select all that apply.
options: The commit limit is exhausted: RAM and the page file are already promised
A process in a container hit the GC heap limit
A 32-bit process couldn’t find a contiguous range of addresses
Too many threads are waiting on a lock
The garbage collector is off by default
cards.explain: Waiting on a lock costs no memory, and the garbage collector is always on. The other three are the classics: the memory is promised, you hit your own ceiling, or there were no consecutive addresses.

cards.q: A 64-bit process calls VirtualAlloc with MEM_RESERVE for 1 GB a hundred times and writes nothing. What grew?
options: Only the virtual size
The working set, by 100 GB
Private bytes, by 100 GB
Nothing: Windows refuses on the second call
cards.explain: A reservation is only addresses. 100 GB fits easily into 128 TB of user space, and no commit or RAM is used.

lessons.title: The stack and CPU caches
lessons.sub: The stack limit, cache lines and locality

cards.title: A thread’s stack is a range claimed in advance
cards.body:
Every thread has its own stack. It’s a reserved range of addresses that gets committed bit by bit as the stack grows (it grows downward, toward lower addresses). Allocating on the stack just moves the stack pointer, which makes it almost free.

The size is set up front and doesn’t change:

  • for the main thread of a Windows program it’s usually 1 MB, a value written into the exe header;
  • for the main thread on Linux it follows ulimit -s, usually 8 MB;
  • for threads created by .NET the runtime picks the default, and it depends on the OS and the version. Need a different one? Pass it to the constructor: new Thread(work, maxStackSize).
cards.deep: Check the exact defaults for new threads on your own platform: on Linux the runtime doesn’t inherit the main thread’s 8 MB but sets its own size, around one and a half megabytes. On Linux and macOS the DOTNET_DefaultStackSize environment variable changes it (a hexadecimal number of bytes). The thread pool creates its threads with the default size, so deep recursion inside a request handler runs into exactly that limit.

cards.title: What goes into a stack frame
cards.body:
Every method call adds a frame. It holds:

  • the return address and saved registers;
  • arguments that didn’t fit into registers;
  • local value types: int, double, whole structs;
  • local references, 8 bytes of address, while the object itself is on the heap;
  • stackalloc buffers.

What isn’t on the stack: class instances, variables captured by a lambda (they move into a closure object on the heap), and locals of an async method that live across an await (they become fields of the state machine).
cards.deep: This is a model, not a promise: the JIT can keep a local only in a register and never touch the stack, and it can spread the fields of a small struct across registers. The opposite happens too: in .NET 9–10 the JIT learned to place objects that never leave the method on the stack in some cases (escape analysis). "Classes live on the heap" is still the right model, but the JIT chooses the actual location.

cards.q: What ends up in the stack frame of Draw? Select all that apply.
options: The whole struct p
The reference list, 8 bytes
The List<int> object itself
The 64 bytes of buf
The list’s internal array
cards.explain: The List<int> object and its internal array are on the heap; the stack holds only the reference to the list. The struct and the stackalloc buffer sit right in the frame, unless the JIT moved something into registers.

cards.title: The guard page and StackOverflowException
cards.body:
Just below the committed part of the stack sits a guard page. Touch it and the OS commits the next page and moves the guard further down. That’s how the stack grows on demand.

When the stack reaches the end of its reservation, there’s nowhere left to grow: a stack overflow. In .NET a StackOverflowException can’t be caught: the runtime terminates the process immediately. Neither catch nor finally runs.

Typical causes: infinite recursion, recursion over deep data (a long chain, a degenerate tree), a huge stackalloc. The rule: if recursion depth depends on input, rewrite the traversal with an explicit Stack<T> or check the headroom with RuntimeHelpers.EnsureSufficientExecutionStack().
cards.deep: EnsureSufficientExecutionStack throws InsufficientExecutionStackException when little stack is left; that’s an ordinary exception you can catch. There’s also a version without an exception: TryEnsureSufficientExecutionStack. Recursive parsers and expression compilers protect themselves this way. On Linux the guard page is a protected area: touching it raises SIGSEGV, the runtime recognizes the overflow, prints a message and terminates the process.

cards.q: A chain of 10 million nodes. Which line won’t work the way the author intended?
cards.explain: Ten million nested calls won’t fit on the stack, and StackOverflowException can’t be caught: the process will terminate. Walk the chain with a loop instead.

cards.title: Caches: memory is far, the cache is near
cards.body:
The CPU works faster than RAM can answer, so caches sit between them. Orders of magnitude for latency (exact numbers depend on the CPU):

  • L1: about 1 ns, tens of KB per core;
  • L2: a few ns, from hundreds of KB to a couple of MB per core;
  • L3: on the order of 10 ns, tens of MB shared by all cores;
  • RAM: on the order of 100 ns.

Memory arrives in the cache not byte by byte but in cache lines of 64 bytes. Read one int and the 15 next to it come along. And if you read sequentially, the prefetcher spots the pattern and pulls in the next lines ahead of time.
cards.deep: In cycles at 3–4 GHz: L1 is 4–5 cycles, L2 around 12–15, L3 a few dozen, RAM hundreds. 64 bytes is the line size on x86-64 and most ARM CPUs; on Apple M-series chips it’s 128 bytes. Address translation is cached too, in the TLB, and scattered access over a large amount of memory misses both caches at once.

cards.q: Order these from fastest to slowest
items: Hard page fault from an SSD
cards.explain: A register is a fraction of a nanosecond, L1 about 1 ns, L3 on the order of 10 ns, RAM on the order of 100 ns, a soft fault on the order of a microsecond, a hard fault from an SSD tens to hundreds of microseconds.

cards.title: An array of structs versus an array of references
cards.body:
If Point is a struct of two ints, a Point[] stores the points back to back, 8 bytes each: 8 points per cache line, and a traversal walks straight through memory.

If Point is a class, the array stores only references. Each point is a separate object: 16 bytes of overhead (the header and the type pointer) plus 8 bytes of data. To read pts[i].X you have to load the reference and follow it. Freshly created objects often sit next to each other, but after the program has run for a while and collections have happened, that’s not guaranteed.

For a million points: structs are about 8 MB read sequentially; classes are 8 MB of references plus about 24 MB of objects, and each hop can cost a cache miss.
cards.deep: The next step is a "struct of arrays": if a loop reads only X, keep X in one array and Y in another, and every cache line carries 16 useful numbers instead of 8. ECS engines and vectorization with Vector<T> are built on this. The price is less convenient code, so it’s done only in hot loops, after measuring.

cards.task: Step through both versions: where do the points lie in one block, and where do you have to follow a reference to each?

steps.note: An array of structs is one object. Room for all three points is right inside it, back to back.
The point is written straight into the slot. Neighboring slots are neighboring bytes, in the same cache line.
No new objects: a traversal reads memory strictly in sequence.
One object in total: 24 bytes of points in one block.
An array of classes stores only references, 8 bytes each. All null for now.
Each point is a separate object with its own header. The array holds just the address.
To read X, the CPU first reads the reference and then follows it: a second memory access.
Four objects in total. Where the points end up after collections is not the array’s call.

cards.q: Why is this traversal several times slower than with the loops swapped?
options: Elements adjacent in i are 16 KB apart: every read is a new cache line
A multidimensional array checks bounds twice
Adding longs is slower than adding ints
It isn’t: loop order doesn’t matter
cards.explain: In C# an int[,] is stored row by row: m[i, j] and m[i, j + 1] are neighbors. A row is 4096 × 4 bytes = 16 KB. The last index should change in the inner loop; then the traversal is sequential and one cache line serves 16 reads.

cards.title: False sharing: threads get in each other’s way without sharing data
cards.body:
Two threads each count into their own slot: the first writes to counts[0], the second to counts[1]. There’s no race and the result is correct. Yet it runs slower than a single thread.

The reason: the slots are adjacent and sit in the same cache line. To write, a core must own the line exclusively. Every write by one core takes the line away from the other, and it bounces between their caches. This is false sharing.

Remedies: accumulate in a local variable and write once at the end; keep hot fields at least 64 bytes apart; give each thread its own data.
cards.deep: Core caches coordinate through a coherence protocol (the MESI family): only one core can hold a line it writes to in modified state. Some Intel CPUs fetch lines in pairs, which is why hot fields are sometimes spaced 128 bytes apart. The .NET libraries do this themselves, for example in ConcurrentQueue: the head and tail of the queue are separated by padding.

cards.q: Each thread gets its own counter. Spread the array’s counters across different cache lines
cards.explain: With a 64-byte element, the Value fields of neighboring elements are 64 bytes apart and never land in the same cache line. Size = 8 would give you a plain long array, with eight counters per line.
